# Britecharts documentation

Every guide and API page from https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/, as text. The index is https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/llms.txt.

# Britecharts

Source: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/Britecharts

> Finished, accessible charts that any page, and any agent, can add with one script tag or one validated JSON config.

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@britecharts/core)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@britecharts/core) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-blue.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/Apache-2.0) [![test workflow](https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/actions/workflows/unit-tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/actions/workflows/unit-tests.yml) [![GitHub pull requests](https://img.shields.io/github/issues-pr-raw/britecharts/britecharts)](https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Aopen+sort%3Aupdated-desc) [![jsDelivr hits](https://data.jsdelivr.com/v1/package/npm/@britecharts/core/badge)](https://www.jsdelivr.com/package/npm/@britecharts/core)

[![PRs Welcome](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-welcome-brightgreen.svg)](https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) [![All Contributors](https://img.shields.io/badge/all_contributors-8-orange.svg?style=flat-square)](https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/Britecharts#contributors-) [![Twitter Follow](https://img.shields.io/twitter/follow/britecharts.svg?style=social&label=Follow)](https://twitter.com/Britecharts/followers)

<br/>

Britecharts is a library of finished [D3.js][d3] charts: bar, line, donut, stacked and grouped bar, stacked area, scatter plot, heatmap, sparkline, bullet and brush, plus a tooltip and a legend. You choose a chart, give it data and a few settings, and get a polished, interactive, accessible chart that works the same in plain HTML, any framework or React.

## Why Britecharts

### Finished charts, not a grammar
Grammar libraries hand you scales, marks and axes to assemble. Britecharts hands you a bar chart. Every chart shares one vocabulary (`width`, `colorSchema`, `isLoading`, `numberFormat`, `exportChart`, `a11yTitle`) and comes with loading and empty states, animation, tooltips and export already built. There are fewer ways to go wrong, for people and for coding agents alike.

### Accessible by default, and free
Every chart is accessible without any setup:
-   🔊 **Named for screen readers**, with its data as a table they can read cell by cell.
-   ⌨️ **Keyboard navigable**: tab to a chart, move between data points with the arrow keys, and the tooltip follows focus.
-   🎞 **Still when the reader asks for reduced motion.**
-   🎨 **A colour-blind-safe palette**, Okabe–Ito, one setting away.

Commercial libraries charge per seat for this set. In Britecharts it is on by default, and each part can be turned off.

### One script tag or one config, in any page
The vanilla core runs anywhere: a server-rendered template, a static site, a Web Component, or an AI sandbox that only allows CDN scripts. The same chart is available as a framework-agnostic wrapper and as a React component. And because a chart is a name, a configuration and data, it can be written down as a JSON spec that a schema checks before it's drawn.

### Made for coding agents too
Agents write Britecharts correctly on the first try more often when the library helps them:
-   📄 **[llms.txt][llms-txt]** and **llms-full.txt** describe every chart and accessor.
-   🧠 **An agent skill** ships inside `@britecharts/core`, with each chart's data shape, accessors and common traps.
-   ✅ **A JSON Schema for every chart's spec**, so an editor or an agent can validate a config without running it.
-   💬 **Errors that say how to fix them**: a misspelt key gets "did you mean `height`?" and a link to the chart's API page, and a value of the wrong type says what it should be.

### Charting since 2015
Britecharts started at Eventbrite in May 2015. Version 1 reached npm in March 2017, and version 2 followed that August. Since then, 55 people have contributed code and the repository has earned over 3,700 stars on GitHub. Version 2 is still installed about 5,000 times a week.

Version 3 keeps the idea that made those charts last: a chart is a function you configure and then call on your data. It rebuilds everything around it in TypeScript, with accessibility, theming, React components and tools for coding agents.

## What's New in Version 3

Version 3 is a rewrite of Britecharts in TypeScript, on D3 v7, as three packages: [`@britecharts/core`][core-package], [`@britecharts/wrappers`][wrappers-package] and [`@britecharts/react`][react-package].

-   **Accessibility built in.** Named charts, [data tables and keyboard navigation][a11y-howto], reduced motion and the Okabe–Ito palette, all on by default.
-   **[Theming and dark mode][theming-howto]** with standard CSS. Every colour around the data is a `--bc-*` custom property, and the charts follow the page's `color-scheme` through `light-dark()`.
-   **[Export to SVG or PNG][export-howto]** from one call: `exportChart('chart.svg')`.
-   **[Chart specs and JSON Schemas][spec-howto]**, generated from the TypeScript types, with value checks in the wrappers.
-   **TypeScript types** for every chart's data, configuration and React props.
-   **Every chart in every package**, the brush and heatmap included, and **one tooltip** for all of them.
-   **Responsive by default**: every svg scales to fit its container, with no resize listeners.
-   **Negative values** in the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, brush and scatter plot charts, and **loading states** on every chart.
-   **Smaller bundles**: ES modules that tree-shake, so an app only ships the charts it imports.

Coming from version 2? Read the [migration guide][migration-guide].

## Quick Start

### Try it in your browser

[Open a running example on StackBlitz][try-page], in plain JavaScript or React, with nothing to install. Each draws a bar chart and a line chart with their tooltips, switches to dark mode, and moves through the data with the keyboard.

### From a CDN, with no build step

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css" />
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js"></script>

<div class="bar-container"></div>

<script>
    core.bar()
        .height(300)
        .a11yTitle('Signups by plan')
        .tooltip(core.miniTooltip())
        .render('.bar-container', [
            { name: 'Pro', value: 412 },
            { name: 'Team', value: 236 },
            { name: 'Free', value: 1200 },
        ]);
</script>
```

The bundle includes d3, so the page needs no other script.

### From npm

```bash
npm install @britecharts/core
```

```js
import { bar, miniTooltip } from '@britecharts/core';
import '@britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css';

bar()
    .isHorizontal(true)
    .height(300)
    .a11yTitle('Signups by plan')
    .tooltip(miniTooltip())
    .render('.bar-container', data);
```

`render` takes a CSS selector, an element or a d3 selection, and draws again with new data when you call it again. If you already use d3, `select('.bar-container').datum(data).call(barChart)` works too.

### With React

```bash
npm install @britecharts/react
```

```jsx
import { Bar } from '@britecharts/react';

<Bar data={data} isHorizontal a11yTitle="Signups by plan" />;
```

In an app set up with [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com), one command adds a chart that follows your theme and its dark mode, with [one registry item per chart][shadcn-howto]:

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/bar-chart.json
```

To use Britecharts with another framework, use the `create`, `update` and `destroy` methods of the [wrappers package][wrappers-package]. For Angular, check out [ngx-britecharts][angularwrapper].

### As a JSON spec

```json
{
    "$schema": "https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/schema/v3/bar.json",
    "chart": "bar",
    "config": { "isHorizontal": true, "a11yTitle": "Signups by plan" },
    "data": [{ "name": "Pro", "value": 412 }]
}
```

Editors validate and complete it from the schema, and `BarWrapper.create(element, spec.data, spec.config)` draws it.

## Charts

Every chart shares the common accessors (`width`, `height`, `margin`, `colorSchema`, `isLoading`, `a11yTitle` and so on) and adds its own:

-   [API][line-docs], [Demo][linechart-story] Line Chart
-   [API][bar-docs], [Demo][barchart-story] Bar Chart
-   [API][donut-docs], [Demo][donutchart-story] Donut Chart
-   [API][stacked-bar-docs], [Demo][stackedbarchart-story] Stacked Bar Chart
-   [API][grouped-bar-docs], [Demo][groupedbarchart-story] Grouped Bar Chart
-   [API][stacked-area-docs], [Demo][stackedareachart-story] Stacked Area Chart
-   [API][scatter-docs], [Demo][scatterplot-story] Scatter Plot
-   [API][heatmap-docs], [Demo][heatmap-story] Heatmap
-   [API][sparkline-docs], [Demo][sparklinechart-story] Sparkline Chart
-   [API][bullet-docs], [Demo][bulletchart-story] Bullet Chart
-   [API][brush-docs], [Demo][brushchart-story] Brush Chart
-   [API][tooltip-docs], [Demo][linechart-story] Tooltip, and its [single-value preset][mini-tooltip-docs]
-   [API][legend-docs], [Demo][donutchart-story] Legend

[line-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/line
[bar-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/bar
[donut-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/donut
[stacked-bar-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/stacked-bar
[grouped-bar-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/grouped-bar
[bullet-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/bullet
[brush-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/brush
[scatter-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/scatter-plot
[heatmap-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/heatmap
[sparkline-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/sparkline
[stacked-area-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/stacked-area
[mini-tooltip-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/tooltip#minitooltip-the-single-value-preset
[tooltip-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/tooltip
[legend-docs]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/legend

Britecharts is built with the [reusable chart pattern][mike-chart] on plain D3.js code you can read, fork and modify, and every chart is covered by unit tests and by browser tests in real consumer apps. To customise the look, see [Styling Britecharts][stylingbritecharts].

## Community Roadmap
This project is in active development. We want your input about what is important, for that, add your votes using the 👍 reaction:
* [Top Feature Requests](https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed+sort%3Areactions-%2B1-desc+label%3Atype%3Afeature+-label:status:completed)
* [Documentation Requests](https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed+sort%3Areactions-%2B1-desc+label%3Atype%3Adocumentation+-label:status:completed)
* [Top Bugs](https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed+sort%3Areactions-%2B1-desc+label%3Atype%3Abug+-label:status:completed)

## How to Contribute

Whether you're helping us fix bugs, improving the docs, or spreading the word, we'd love to have you as part of the Britecharts community!

To give your feedback, you can open a new issue. You can also find us in the [D3.js slack group][d3slack], in the **#tool-britecharts** channel. We are looking for contributors and committers, so if you want to become a part of this project, check the [contributing guide][contributing-guide] for ideas on contributing and get started today!

## Code of Conduct

Britecharts is dedicated to building a welcoming, diverse, and safe community. We expect everyone participating in the Britecharts community to abide by our [Code of Conduct][code-conduct]. Please read it and follow it.

## Acknowledgments

[Sun Dai][sunsdribble] designs Britecharts, and two books inspired the code, [Developing a D3.js Edge][d3-edge] and [Mastering D3.js][mastering-d3]. It also leveraged a significant number of examples and articles from the [D3.js][d3] community overall.

# Getting Started Using Britecharts

Source: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/tutorials/getting-started

We created Britecharts to help users consume and create D3.js charts. It leverages the *Reusable API*, a code pattern to encapsulate D3.js charts. This pattern produces chart objects that can be configured, reused and composed to build data visualizations.

In this tutorial, we will *create a simple data visualization using Britecharts*. You will learn how to load Britecharts, instantiate and configure a chart and plot it within a container with a data set.

## Downloading Britecharts
To use a Britechart, we need to install the library. In this tutorial, we are going to use a simple CDN link to install it. For that, create a simple HTML file and add this script tag:

```html
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js"
        type="text/javascript"></script>
```
The bundle has every chart, and the d3 modules they use, so the page needs no other script.

We also need to load the styling of our chart, and we do it similarly by accesing the CDN link:
```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css" type="text/css" />
```

## Setting up Container, Dataset and Chart
To create a container, we add a div in the DOM with a class:
```html
<div class="bar-container"></div>
```

We instantiate a new chart by calling the function bar() inside the `core` object in the global namespace:
```js
const barChart = core.bar();
```
We need a simple dataset to render the bar chart. We can find the right format of the data by visiting the [API documentation][barChartAPI] for the bar chart component. Developers need to find the data definition at the top of the page; in this case, it is a link labeled [BarChartData][barChartDataSchema]. It looks like this:
```json
[
    {
        value: 1,
        name: 'glittering'
    },
    {
        value: 1,
        name: 'luminous'
    }
]
```
We can extend that definition to have some more bars, for example:
```js
const barData = [
    { name: 'Luminous', value: 2 },
    { name: 'Glittering', value: 5 },
    { name: 'Intense', value: 4 },
    { name: 'Radiant', value: 3 }
];
```

## Configuring and Rendering the bar chart
We only need to configure our bar chart by calling the accessors. We describe these in the [bar chart API reference][barChartAPI] page. In this tutorial, we set it up as a horizontal bar chart with a height of 400px and a width of 600px:
```js
barChart
    .margin({left: 100})
    .isHorizontal(true)
    .height(400)
    .width(600);
```
Notice how we tweaked a bit the left margin in order to allow space for our left aligned labels to render.

We only need to render our configured bar chart into the container, with the data:
```js
barChart.render('.bar-container', barData);
```
`render` takes a CSS selector, an element or a d3 selection. Calling it again with new data redraws the chart.
To render a simple bar chart:

![Simple Bar Chart][barChartImg]

Here is all the code inside the `<body>` tag of our HTML file:
```html
<div class="bar-container"></div>

<script>
    // Instantiate bar chart
    const barChart = core.bar();

    // Create Dataset with proper shape
    const barData = [
        { name: 'Luminous', value: 2 },
        { name: 'Glittering', value: 5 },
        { name: 'Intense', value: 4 },
        { name: 'Radiant', value: 3 }
    ];

    // Configure chart
    barChart
        .margin({left: 100})
        .isHorizontal(true)
        .height(400)
        .width(600);

    barChart.render('.bar-container', barData);
</script>
```
In version 3 of Britecharts, the rendered charts are already responsive, so you can stretch and compress the viewport size to see the chart react.

You can check the full code of this tutorial [in this file][simpleBarChartTutorialHTML] and the [tutorial working here][simpleBarChartTutorial].

## Summary
In this tutorial, we have seen how to load Britecharts with a CDN link and how to draw a simple chart. We did this by checking the API Reference page for the chart and its data schema and by creating the elements needed in the HTML file.

To keep on learning more about Britecharts, you can follow our [Composing Your First Data Visualization tutorial][composingDataviz] or read abbout how to [install Britecharts in your project][installingBritecharts]. You can also check out our [Documentation Homepage][home] and our [kitchen sink][demos] to see all the available charts.

If you are excited about Britecharts, want to add more configurable properties or even create your own chart, please check our [Contributing Guide][contribute]. In it, we walk you through the development environment setup, running our docs and demos and creating new Pull Requests.

[home]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/
[demos]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/storybook/
[contribute]: https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md
[barChartAPI]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/bar
[barChartDataSchema]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/bar#exportsbarchartdata--arrayobject
[barChartImg]: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/britecharts/britecharts/main/packages/docs/static/img/tutorial/simple-bar-chart.png
[simpleBarChartTutorialHTML]: https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/blob/main/packages/docs/docs/tutorials/html/tutorial-simple-bar-chart.html
[simpleBarChartTutorial]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/storybook/core/?path=/story/charts-bar--playground

# Installing Britecharts

Source: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/tutorials/installing-britecharts

In the [Getting Started Guide][gettingStarted] you saw how to use Britecharts using a CDN link. This is not the only way. Britecharts allows developers to add the library following several strategies.

In this tutorial, you will learn to install Britecharts in your project by using different approaches:
* Using a package manager (npm or pnpm)
* Using the CDN links
* Building the Source Code

## Install with NPM
The recommended way of installing Britecharts is to use npm or pnpm:
```
npm install --save @britecharts/core
```
Or, using pnpm:
```
pnpm add @britecharts/core
```
Notice this requires you to have in place a bundling system (Webpack, Parcel, Rollup, or Similar). If you want to drop a script in an HTML file and start working, use the CDN way below.

To use the modules within your JavaScript code, you will follow a different approach depending on the type of modules you are using:
```js
// For CommonJS modules
const { bar } = require('@britecharts/core');

// For ES modules
import { bar } from '@britecharts/core';

bar().render('.bar-container', data);
```

The charts draw with `render`, so you don't need d3 in your own code. If you do use d3, `select('.bar-container').datum(data).call(barChart)` works too.

When loading the styles, you have two options, loading the whole stylesheet of the library:
```html
<link type="text/css" rel="stylesheet" href="node_modules/@britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css">
```

Or loading only the styles for the current chart plus the common Britecharts styles:
```html
<link type="text/css" rel="stylesheet" href="node_modules/@britecharts/core/dist/styles/charts/common.min.css">
<link type="text/css" rel="stylesheet" href="node_modules/@britecharts/core/dist/styles/charts/bar.min.css">
```

## Download from the CDN
To import the latest bundle (3.x.x version), use this URL:
```
https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js
```
This bundle attaches to the global `window` object a JavaScript object called `britecharts`. Within it, you can find the charts and helpers you need.

With Britecharts, you can also download individual bundles of the charts and helpers. To do this, you can [browse all CDN files][jsDelivrDist], browsing inside the `umd` folder to find the chart URL you need.

You can see the CDN links in action in:
* our [CDN demo page][cdnDemo]
* this [JSBin][jsbinSandbox] sandbox project
* this [CodePen][codepenSandbox] pen

## Building the source code
To build the soure code, you need first to get the code. You can do it by cloning or downloading it from Github.com. You can clone the git repository by running:
```
   git clone https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts.git
```
Or download the source code by navigating to the [Release Page][githubReleases] and click in the latest's release `zip` or `tar.gz` links.

Then, you would need to install the dependencies and build the project. Check the [Contributing Guide][contributingGuide] to learn about this process.

## Summary
In this tutorial, you have seen three different ways of adding Britecharts to  your site or web application.

To keep on learning more about Britecharts, you can follow our [Composing Your First Data Visualization][composingDataviz] or our [Styling Britecharts][stylingBritecharts] tutorials. You can also check out our [documentation Homepage][home] and our [kitchen sink][demos] to see all the available charts.

If you are excited about Britecharts, want to add more configurable properties or even create your own chart, please check our [Contributing Guide][contributingGuide]. In it, we walk you through the development environment setup, running our docs and demos and creating new Pull Requests.

[jsDelivrDist]: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/
[cdnDemo]: https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/blob/main/packages/integration/consumers/vanilla/cdn-jsdelivr.html
[jsbinSandbox]: https://jsbin.com/wativun/1/edit?html,js,output
[codepenSandbox]: https://codepen.io/Golodhros/pen/PprGeP?editors=1010
[contributingGuide]: https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md
[githubReleases]: https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/releases

# Composing Your First Data Visualization

Source: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/tutorials/composing-dataviz

In the [Getting Started Guide][gettingStarted], we saw how to set up a responsive Bar chart using Britecharts. This tutorial was easy to follow; however, most of the times our real-world requirements include other components to help communicate our data.

In this tutorial, we will create a complex data visualization. You will learn how to draw a line chart with a tooltip, how to add a legend and a data filtering tool using a brush chart.

## Rendering a line chart
Let's build on top of the Bar Chart tutorial by using its code structure. We load the same bundle, which has every chart:
```html
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js"></script>
```
Then, we will instantiate a line chart:
```js
const lineChart = core.line();
```
The shape of our data changed as well. We need to check the [line chart data schema][lineChartDataSchema] for this chart. In our case, it looks like this:
```js
const lineData = {
    "data": [
        {
            "value": 0,
            "name": -1,
            "topicName": "Vivid",
            "date": "2016-08-01T00:00:00-07:00"
        },
        {
            "value": 3,
            "name": 2,
            "topicName": "Radiant",
            "date": "2016-08-01T00:00:00-07:00"
        },
        ...
    ]
};
```

Before configuring the chart, we figure out the container's size to apply it as the chart width:
```js
const container = document.querySelector('.line-container');
const containerWidth = container.getBoundingClientRect().width;
```

Configuring and rendering the line chart follows an identical approach as with the bar chart:
```js
lineChart
    .margin({bottom: 50})
    .height(400)
    .width(containerWidth);

lineChart.render(container, lineData);
```

That renders the following chart:
![Simple Line Chart][lineChartImg]

## Adding a Tooltip
Now that we have a line chart working, we are going to add a tooltip to allow users to check the specific values on each date. We start by instantiating a new [Tooltip component][tooltipAPIReference]:
```js
const chartTooltip = core.tooltip();
```

Then we give it to the line chart:
```js
lineChart
    .margin({bottom: 50})
    .height(400)
    .width(containerWidth)
    .tooltip(chartTooltip);

lineChart.render(container, lineData);
```
The chart does the rest. It shows the tooltip when the pointer enters the chart, or when the keyboard moves to a date, updates it as they move, and hides it when they leave. It draws the tooltip in its hover marker, and tells the tooltip which fields of its data to read.
After the previous code, we will see a tooltip like the following:
![Line Chart with Tooltip][lineChartTooltipImg]

## Drawing a Legend
Up to now, we have been working with a dataset that contains only one topic. But what happens if we have two topics? In this section, we will update our data to contain another set of entries. We add a legend component to show our users which line corresponds to which topic.

First, we make a copy of the topic we already have and change some values. We named the new topic "Radiant," and due to our default color schema, it shows as a dark green line.

Now we instantiate our new [legend component][legendAPIReference]:
```js
const chartLegend = core.legend();
```
The same way as we needed a container for the chart, we require another for the legend:
```html
<div class="legend-container"></div>
```

The legend is a component that depends on the data and in a specific data shape. We check the Legend data schema, and it needs to be:
```json
[
    {
        id: 1,
        quantity: 2,
        name: 'glittering'
    },
    {
        id: 2,
        quantity: 3,
        name: 'luminous'
    }
]
```
As we want to show an inline legend, which doesn't show the quantity, we only need one entry per line, with its name, an id and a quantity of zero. Here is how we create that data:
```js
// One entry per line: every point repeats its line's name and topicName
const legendData = Array.from(
    new Map(
        lineData.data.map(({ topicName, name }) => [
            name,
            { id: name, name: topicName, quantity: 0 },
        ])
    ).values()
);
```
And we are ready to configure and draw the legend:
```js
chartLegend
    .width(containerWidth)
    .height(60)
    .isHorizontal(true);

chartLegend.render('.legend-container', legendData);
```
Note how we have used the container width to position the legend in the center. You can see the rest of the options of the legend component in its [API reference page][legendAPIReference].

The resulting chart is:
![Line Chart with Legend][lineChartLegendImg]

## Filtering Data with a Brush
Our current data is not that extensive, but in theory, our line chart could render datasets of any size. This could be a problem as we could get into a position where the data points get too close, and our users can't see the details of the data. One way of fixing this is by allowing to filter data, and the way we do it visually is by using a brush chart.

In this section, we go over the process of adding a brush chart to our visualization, allowing to drag and drop a section of the data to zoom in that period.

### Creating the brush chart
Let's first instantiate the brush chart:
```js
const chartBrush = core.brush();
```
We would need to add its container to the DOM:
```html
<div class="brush-container"></div>
```

Now, as we did before, we are going to check the [Brush Chart API][brushChartAPIReference] and its [data schema][brushChartDataSchema]. The data needs to look like this:
```json
[
    {
        value: 1,
        date: "2011-01-06T00:00:00Z"
    },
    {
        value: 2,
        date: "2011-01-07T00:00:00Z"
    }
]
```
So, in order to get this data shape, we will need to do some modifications to our line chart data:
```js
const brushData = lineData.data
    .reduce(consolidateDatesReducer, []);
```
In the first reducer function, we obtain the entries by date, keeping only date and values. On the second one, we remove duplicated dates and sum up the values to have an aggregate of them. You can check the details of these functions in the [final code][composingDatavizTutorialHTML].

Now we are ready to configure and render our brush using the usual pattern:
```js
chartBrush
    .width(containerWidth)
    .height(100)
    .xAxisFormat(chartBrush.axisTimeCombinations.DAY_MONTH)
    .margin({top:0, bottom: 40, left: 50, right: 30});

chartBrush.render('.brush-container', brushData);
```
Notice that we are setting the x-axis format to a constant called `DAY_MONTH` within the axisTimeCombinations object. This `xAxisFormat` option is a way for us to select a date format that works for our data. In this case, it is the day of the month, as the default one (hours) was showing the same hour every day.

This code renders a simple Brush chart:
![Simple Brush Chart][brushChartImg]

This chart only serves as an overview of the sum of data in our dataset. What we want to do is, when we drag and drop a section of the brush, select that portion of our dataset and re-render the line chart with it.

For that, we listen to the `customBrushEnd` event on the brush, that returns the period of the brush selection. We take the beginning and end of that period and filter our original data with them. Finally, we apply it to the line chart and re-render. Here is the code for it:
```js
chartBrush
    .width(containerWidth)
    .height(100)
    .xAxisFormat(chartBrush.axisTimeCombinations.DAY_MONTH)
    .margin({ top: 0, bottom: 40, left: 50, right: 30 })
    .on('customBrushEnd', ([brushStart, brushEnd]) => {
        if (brushStart && brushEnd) {
            let filteredLineData = filterData(brushStart, brushEnd);

            lineChart.render(container, filteredLineData);
        }
    });
```
This results in a data visualization where we can focus on different sections of the data, and use our tooltip to see the values on those:
![Line with Brush, Tooltip and Legend][lineBrushTooltipLegendImg]

Here is the filtering logic for your reference:
```js
const isInRange = (startDate, endDate, {date}) => new Date(date) >= startDate && new Date(date) <= endDate;
const filterData = (brushStart, brushEnd) => {
    // Copy the data
    let data = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(lineData));

    data.data = data.data.filter(isInRange.bind(null, brushStart, brushEnd));

    return data;
};
```

You can see the full code of this tutorial [in this file][composingDatavizTutorialHTML] and the [tutorial working here][composingDatavizTutorial].

## Summary
In this tutorial, we have seen how we can use different support components like the legend and tooltip to provide information about our charts. We also saw how we could use the brush chart to provide a high-level view of our dataset. We saw how to configure the brush to filter the data and how to reload our main chart with this new data.

To learn more, you can read our [Styling Britecharts tutorial][stylingBritecharts] or check our demos and documentation. If you decided to use Britecharts in your project, you could follow the [Installing Britecharts tutorial][installingBritecharts] to learn what's the better way to use Britecharts. Check also the [Topics page][topicsIndex] to learn more about our approach.

If you are excited about Britecharts, want to add more configurable properties or even create your own chart, please check our [Contributing Guide][contribute]. In it, we walk you through the development environment setup, running our docs and demos and creating new Pull Requests.

[gettingStarted]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/tutorials/getting-started

# Styling Britecharts

Source: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/tutorials/styling-charts

In the [Getting Started Guide][gettingStarted] and the [Composing Your First Data Visualization tutorial][composingDataviz] we saw how to create and configure Britecharts. We have created beatiful charts, however, users have specific branding and styling needs that want to get in their charts to adapt to their user interfaces.

In this tutorial, we will go over the **different options we have to customize Britechart**s. You will learn how you can use Britechart's color schemas to change the charts colors or customize your own. We will also see how to override the CSS styles that come with Britecharts and how to update the fonts.

## Applying a color palette
Let's look at some customization options we have available for Britecharts. The first one is the color schemas and gradients. You can find some of them in our [Color Palettes demo page][colorPalettesDemo].

To get us started with a tutorial, we are going to take our [Getting Started tutorial][gettingStarted] code and create [a new HTML file][stylingBritechartsHTML] based on it.

We will start from the code we got at the end of that tutorial, removing the responsive part:
```js
// Instantiate Bar Chart
const barChart = core.bar();

// Create Dataset with proper shape
const barData = [
    { name: 'Luminous', value: 2 },
    { name: 'Glittering', value: 5 },
    { name: 'Intense', value: 4 },
    { name: 'Radiant', value: 3 }
];

// Configure chart
barChart
    .margin({ left: 100 })
    .isHorizontal(true)
    .height(400)
    .width(600);

barChart.render('.bar-container', barData);
```

Starting with this bar chart, we want to customize the color palette. The color schemas come with the bundle, as `core.colors`, so we can set the color schema of the bar chart by doing:
```js
// Configure chart
barChart
    .colorSchema(core.colors.colorSchemas.orange)
    .margin({ left: 100 })
    .isHorizontal(true)
    .height(400)
    .width(600);
```
That renders an orange bar chart:
![Orange Bar Chart][orangeBarChartImg]

The different color palettes we provide in Britecharts are ubicated within the `colorSchemas` object. You can see their colors them in the [demo page][colorPalettesDemo].

When we look at the palettes code, they are just an array of nine hexadecimal values. For example:
```js
// Britecharts palette
["#6aedc7", "#39c2c9", "#ffce00", "#ffa71a", "#f866b9", "#998ce3"]
```
Which means that if you want to customize your charts color palette, you only need to pass an array of hexadecimal colors into the `.colorSchema` accessors.

## Using a color gradient
Some Britecharts use a color gradient for their lines (line, sparkline and stacked area charts) or for the body of the chart (brush).

You can find these color gradients in `core.colors.colorGradients` and similarly, they are an array of colors. However, in this case they are only two colors, one for the beginning and another for the end of the gradient.

## Overriding default styles
Whenever we want to change the font family, font sizes or any other styling detail of our charts, we can do so by creating CSS overrides. As an example, let's change the font of our bar chart.

We'll begin by looking for a new font in [Google Fonts][gFonts]. I am a fan of the font `Oswald`, so let's add it to our tutorial by including this link tag in the header:
```html
<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css?family=Oswald:600" rel="stylesheet">
```
Now, we need to set up a style override. For that, we can inspect our SVG elements with the dev tools of our browser. In this case, we see that the `font-family` attribute is set by the `.britechart` class. To override it, we need to add a `style` tag after the link that loads the default britecharts styling and inside the tag, include following code:
```html
<style>
    .britechart,
    .tick text {
        font-family: 'Oswald', sans-serif;
    }
</style>
```
This CSS code will override the `font-family` definition for both the whole chart and the specific tick text of our axes. If we also change the color schema to the red palette, we get this chart:
![Red Bar Chart][redBarChartImg]

We could follow the same steps to style most of Britechart's styling. One caveat is that, given that Britecharts is an SVG based library, the styling of SVG elements is sometimes different. In those cases, check out this [SVG styling guide][svgReference] to make sure you are updating the right properties.

## Summary
In this tutorial, you saw how you can use Britecharts' color helper to apply color palettes and color gradients to your charts. You also saw you can customize all the elments by using CSS style overrides. You can see the [tutorial code working here][stylingBritechartsTutorial].

To learn more, you can follow our [Composing Your First Data Visualization tutorial][composingDataviz]. You can also check out our [Documentation Homepage][home] and our [kitchen sink][demos] to see all the available charts.

[home]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/
[demos]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/storybook/
[gettingStarted]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/tutorials/getting-started
[composingDataviz]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/tutorials/composing-dataviz
[colorPalettesDemo]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/storybook/core/?path=/story/attributes-colors--color-schemas
[stylingBritechartsHTML]: https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/blob/main/packages/docs/docs/tutorials/html/tutorial-styling-britecharts.html
[stylingBritechartsTutorial]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/tutorials/styling-charts
[orangeBarChartImg]: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/britecharts/britecharts/main/packages/docs/static/img/tutorial/orange-bar-chart.png
[redBarChartImg]: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/britecharts/britecharts/main/packages/docs/static/img/tutorial/red-bar-chart.png

# User How-To Guides

Source: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/how-tos/user-how-to-guides

Our how-to guides are recipes to address specific and critical use cases when working with Britecharts. They assume some knowledge about Britecharts and the library structure. If this is the first time you work with Britecharts, we recommend you to read the [Getting Started Tutorial][gettingStarted] first.

## How to Customize the Chart's Colors
Follow these steps to customize Britecharts' charts to use different color schemas:
1. Find out if your chart supports the `.colorSchema()` configuration, if so, keep on reading
1. Check the [Color Palettes demo page][colorPalettesDemo] and find a palette you like
1. Import the `colors` helper at the top of your file
1. Set the color palette with `.colorSchema(colors.colorSchemas.orange)` or with any other color schema
1. Draw the chart

For readers with colour blindness, use `colors.colorSchemas.okabeIto`. Its eight colours, from Okabe and Ito's palette, stay distinct with the common kinds of colour blindness. Black comes last, so charts with up to seven categories never draw a series in black. Its yellow, orange and sky blue are light on a white background, so the palette suits filled marks such as bars and donut slices better than thin lines. Colour shouldn't be the only thing that tells series apart: a legend or labels help every reader.

Note that in some charts we can only configure a gradient. Use the `colorGradients` object instead of `colorSchemas` within the colors helper. You can explore other options in the source code of the [colors file][colorsHelper].

### Give each category its own colour
A palette assigns colours in order, so a category's colour changes when the data does. To pin one colour to each category, pass `colorMap` an object from category to colour:

```js
barChart.colorMap({
    Shiny: '#39c2c9',
    Blazing: '#fcc870',
});
```

A category the map leaves out keeps its palette colour. Each chart matches the keys against one field of its data:

| Chart | `colorMap` keys match |
| --- | --- |
| Bar, donut, scatter plot, stacked area | `name` |
| Line | `name`, the topic's identifier (not `topicName`) |
| Stacked bar | `stack` |
| Grouped bar | `group` |

The legend takes `colorMap` too: pass it the same object so its entries match the chart. In React, `colorMap` is a prop with the same shape.

## How to Theme a Chart and Support Dark Mode
Everything around the data (text, axes, grid lines, tooltips, the legend, loading skeletons) takes its colour from a CSS custom property. Each defaults to a light and a dark value, picked by the [`color-scheme`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/color-scheme) the chart inherits from your page.

To follow the system's light or dark setting, declare both schemes on your page:

```css
:root {
    color-scheme: light dark;
}
```

To force one, set `color-scheme: light` or `color-scheme: dark` on the page, or on any element around the chart. An app with its own light/dark switch sets it there. A page that declares no colour scheme keeps the charts light, as before.

To change a colour, set its token on the charts:

```css
.britechart {
    --bc-text-muted: #555;
    --bc-background: #10141a; /* the colour behind your charts */
}
```

| Token | Colours |
| --- | --- |
| `--bc-text` | tooltip values and other primary text |
| `--bc-text-muted` | tick labels, data labels, tooltip titles |
| `--bc-text-subtle` | axis titles |
| `--bc-axis` | tick marks, the lines that extend the axes, custom line annotations |
| `--bc-grid`, `--bc-grid-highlight` | grid lines, and a highlighted one |
| `--bc-background` | what is behind the chart: the line chart's drawing mask and an export's background. It defaults to `Canvas`, the page's background in the current scheme; set it if your page uses another. |
| `--bc-surface` | the tooltip box, data point markers, hollow circles, heatmap borders |
| `--bc-border` | the tooltip's border and the hover marker |
| `--bc-skeleton`, `--bc-skeleton-strong` | loading states |
| `--bc-brush-area`, `--bc-brush-area-missing` | the brush's area, and its gaps |
| `--bc-sparkline-area-start`, `--bc-sparkline-area-end` | the sparkline's default area gradient |

The data colours come from `colorSchema` and `colorMap`, not from these tokens. Exports carry the resolved colours, so an image exported in dark mode keeps its dark background. Browsers without `light-dark()` (before 2024) show the light values.

## How to Add a Tooltip to a Chart
Give the chart a tooltip with its `tooltip` setting: `tooltip()` for the line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts, which list one row per topic, or `miniTooltip()` for the bar, heatmap and scatter plot, which show one value. The donut has no tooltip: it shows the hovered slice in its centre instead.

```js
stackedBar()
    .tooltip(tooltip().title('Visits'))
    .render('.js-chart', data);
```

The chart does the rest, on every draw. It shows the tooltip when the pointer or the keyboard reaches a data point, moves it as they move and hides it when they leave. It draws the tooltip in place, and sets the labels that tell the tooltip which fields of its data points to read, unless you set them on the tooltip yourself. Set `tooltip(null)` to remove it. A tooltip belongs to one chart, so give each chart its own.

### Connect a tooltip by hand
To change the data point before the tooltip shows it, connect the tooltip yourself.

Drawing the tooltip by hand takes d3's `select`, which the `tooltip` setting does not need. With npm, run `npm install d3-selection` and import `select` from it. On a CDN page, add `<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/d3-selection@3.0.0/dist/d3-selection.min.js"></script>` and call `d3.select`.

1. Connect the chart's `customMouseOver`, `customMouseMove` and `customMouseOut` events to the tooltip's `show`, `update` and `hide`
1. Tell the tooltip where the chart keeps its data, if the table below lists a setting for it
1. Draw the chart, then call the tooltip on the chart's `.metadata-group` (for the line and stacked area, on `.metadata-group .vertical-marker-container`)

```js
import { stackedBar, tooltip } from '@britecharts/core';
import { select } from 'd3-selection';

const stackedBarChart = stackedBar();
const chartTooltip = tooltip()
    .topicLabel('values')
    .nameLabel('stack');

stackedBarChart
    .on('customMouseOver', chartTooltip.show)
    .on('customMouseMove', chartTooltip.update)
    .on('customMouseOut', chartTooltip.hide)
    .render('.js-chart', data);

select('.js-chart .metadata-group').datum([]).call(chartTooltip);
```

The charts do not all name the fields of the data point they send the tooltip the same way, so some need a setting. The `tooltip` setting sets these for you. By hand, or with React's `Tooltip`, set them yourself; without them, the tooltip shows no rows, rows without their colours, or no value:

| Chart | Tooltip settings | React `Tooltip` props |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Line | none | `topicLabel="topics"` |
| Stacked area | `topicLabel('values')` | none |
| Stacked bar | `topicLabel('values')`, `nameLabel('stack')` | `nameLabel="stack"` |
| Grouped bar | `topicLabel('values')`, `nameLabel('group')` | `nameLabel="group"` |
| Scatter plot | `valueLabel('y')` | `valueLabel="y"` |
| Bar, heatmap | none | none |

React's `Tooltip` starts from `topicLabel('values')`, which is why the line chart is the one that needs a prop there. The [tooltip reference][tooltipAPI] describes each setting, and the [Storybook][storybook] shows each chart with its tooltip configured.

## How to Format Numbers and Dates for Your Language
Three settings control how values read. They do different things, so check which one a chart has in its [API reference][apiReference]:

* `numberFormat` takes a [d3-format specifier][formatSpecifiers], such as `',.2f'` for two decimals with a thousands separator, or `'.0%'` for a percentage. It formats the values on the chart's axes and labels; the tooltip has a `numberFormat` of its own.
* `valueLocale` takes a [d3-format locale definition][formatLocale] and sets the separators and currency those values use. The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar and scatter plot charts have it. The definition needs at least `decimal`, `thousands`, `grouping` and `currency`, or the chart throws.
* `locale` takes a language tag such as `'fr-FR'`, and localizes the dates in the tooltip and the brush with `Intl.DateTimeFormat`.

```js
barChart
    .numberFormat(',.2f')
    .valueLocale({
        decimal: ',',
        thousands: '.',
        grouping: [3],
        currency: ['', ' €'],
    });
// The axis reads 1.000,00 instead of 1,000.00
```

Negative numbers use the typographic minus sign (`−`), as d3-format does. To get the ASCII hyphen back, add `minus: '-'` to the locale definition.

Each chart keeps its `valueLocale` to itself, so two charts on a page can use different ones.

## How to Show a Loading State
Every data chart can draw a skeleton in its own shape while the data loads:
1. Set `isLoading(true)` and draw the chart with whatever data you have, even an empty array
1. When the data arrives, set `isLoading(false)` and draw the chart again with it

```js
barChart.isLoading(true).render('.js-chart', []);

fetchData().then((data) => {
    barChart.isLoading(false).render('.js-chart', data);
});
```

In React, pass `isLoading` together with the data you have, an empty array included, and set it to `false` when the data arrives. With `data={null}`, the component draws nothing at all, skeleton included.

## How to Animate a Chart
Charts draw without animation by default. Set `isAnimated(true)` to animate them as they draw, and `animationDuration` to set how long that takes, in milliseconds (1200 by default):

```js
lineChart.isAnimated(true).animationDuration(600);
```

`animationDuration` does nothing while `isAnimated` is `false`. The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, line, stacked area, donut, heatmap, scatter plot, sparkline and brush charts animate. React components take both as props.

A reader whose system asks for reduced motion (the `prefers-reduced-motion` setting) sees every chart drawn without animation, whatever `isAnimated` is set to. Charts check it each time they draw, so changing the setting applies from the next render. `isAnimated()` still reads back the value you set. The rest of the motion stops too: tooltips appear and move without fading or easing, the legend drops entries without a fade, and a hovered point is highlighted without its bounce.

## How to Export a Chart
Call `exportChart` with a filename to download the chart as it is drawn. The filename picks the format: one ending in `.svg` downloads an svg file, and any other a png. An optional second argument adds a title at the top:

```js
barChart.exportChart('visits.svg', 'Visits by month');
barChart.exportChart('visits.png');
```

The svg keeps the chart's styles inlined, so it looks the same in a design tool or a document, and it stays sharp at any size. `exportChart` returns a promise that resolves once the download starts. In React, every chart component except `Brush` and `Legend` takes the filename as its `exportChart` prop. Setting it downloads the chart once, so set a new filename to download again.

## How to Chart Negative Values
The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, brush and scatter plot charts draw negative values with no setting to turn on:

* The bar charts draw bars below, or to the left of, a zero baseline, and a stacked bar stacks its negative parts down from zero.
* The scatter plot's value axis runs below zero when the data does, and a circle's size shows the size of its value, so -50 draws as large as 50.

The line and stacked area charts plot negative values as they are. Axis labels for negative numbers use the typographic minus sign: see [how to format numbers](https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/how-tos/user-how-to-guides#how-to-format-numbers-and-dates-for-your-language) to change it.

## How to Make a Chart Accessible
For an overview with live charts to try, and how other libraries compare, see [Accessible JavaScript Charts](https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/accessibility).

Every chart gives its svg a role and a name that screen readers announce: "Bar chart" by default. Name it after what it shows, and add a sentence about what it means:

```js
barChart
    .a11yTitle('Monthly visits')
    .a11yDescription('Visits doubled in May');
```

The name goes in an `aria-label`, so browsers do not show it as a tooltip on hover. React components take `a11yTitle` and `a11yDescription` as props.

### Read the data as a table
Every chart but the legend also renders its data as a table, right after its svg, which screen readers reach as a table: they can read it row by row, move along a row or down a column, and hear each cell's headings. It is hidden from sight, takes no room on the page, and is linked from the chart with `aria-details`. Its caption is the chart's name, so set `a11yTitle` and the table is named after it too.

Charts with several series lay it out wide, as a reader would expect: a line chart has a row per date and a column per topic, and a heatmap a row per day and a column per hour.

The table is on by default. If your page already shows the data in an accessible form, turn it off:

```js
barChart.a11yDataTable(false);
```

In React, pass `a11yDataTable={false}`; in the wrappers, `a11yDataTable: false` in the configuration.

### Move through the data with a keyboard
The bar, donut, grouped bar, heatmap, line, scatter plot, stacked area and stacked bar charts can be explored without a pointer. Each chart is one stop in the page's tab order; once it has focus:

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| Right or Left arrow | moves to the next or previous data point: a bar, a slice, a date, a point |
| Down or Up arrow | the same, except on the heatmap, where they move a day |
| Home, End | moves to the first or last point |
| Escape | lets go of the point; leaving the chart does too |

The chart responds as it does to a pointer: the point is highlighted, the tooltip follows focus, and the `customMouseOver`, `customMouseMove` and `customMouseOut` events fire, so your own hover code works from the keyboard too. The browser's focus ring shows which chart has focus.

It is on by default. To take the charts out of the tab order, for example in a list of thumbnails, turn it off:

```js
barChart.a11yKeyboardNavigation(false);
```

In React, pass `a11yKeyboardNavigation={false}`; in the wrappers, `a11yKeyboardNavigation: false` in the configuration.

### Label a bullet chart or a sparkline
The bullet chart and the sparkline draw only their data, with no title: text inside an svg cannot wrap and ignores the page's typography. Put the label in your own markup, next to the chart, and give screen readers the same words:

```html
<h3>CPU load <small>GHz</small></h3>
<div class="js-bullet-chart"></div>
```

```js
bulletChart.a11yTitle('CPU load, GHz').render('.js-bullet-chart', data);
```

## How to Describe a Chart as a Spec and Check It
A chart can be written down as a spec, a plain object with its name, its configuration and its data, which you can store, send from a server, or have a coding agent write:

```json
{
    "$schema": "https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/schema/v3/bar.json",
    "chart": "bar",
    "config": { "isHorizontal": true, "a11yTitle": "Signups by plan" },
    "data": [{ "name": "Pro", "value": 412 }]
}
```

Each chart has a JSON Schema for its spec at `https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/schema/v3/<chart>.json`: `bar`, `brush`, `bullet`, `donut`, `groupedBar`, `heatmap`, `legend`, `line`, `scatterPlot`, `sparkline`, `stackedArea`, `stackedBar` and `tooltip`. They are generated from the charts' TypeScript types, so they list every accessor with its type and description. With the `$schema` line, editors such as VS Code check and complete the spec as you type, and any JSON Schema validator (Ajv, for example) can check one before you draw it.

Draw a spec with the chart's wrapper, which checks it too:

```js
import { BarWrapper } from '@britecharts/wrappers';

BarWrapper.create(element, spec.data, spec.config);
```

A key the chart doesn't have, or a value of the wrong type, throws an error that names each one and says what it should be. Options that take a function, such as the events and the formatting functions, can't be written in JSON: set them from JavaScript.

## How to Add a Chart to a shadcn App
Britecharts has a [shadcn registry](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/registry), so in an app set up with shadcn/ui one command adds a chart:

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/bar-chart.json
```

It copies a component into `components/charts/bar-chart.tsx`, installs `@britecharts/react` and `@britecharts/core`, and adds a rule to your CSS that colours the charts with your shadcn theme: text with `--foreground` and `--muted-foreground`, axes and grid with `--border`, tooltips with `--popover`. The charts follow your app's light and dark modes, and the data keeps Britecharts' palettes. The component is yours to edit.

```tsx
import { BarChart } from '@/components/charts/bar-chart';

<BarChart data={data} height={300} tooltipTitle="Signups" a11yTitle="Signups by plan" />;
```

Each chart fills the width of its container, so put it in an element that has a width, and comes with its tooltip set up. Every other prop is the chart's own, as on its API page.

| Chart | Add it with |
| --- | --- |
| Bar | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/bar-chart.json` |
| Grouped bar | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/grouped-bar-chart.json` |
| Line | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/line-chart.json` |
| Scatter plot | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/scatter-plot.json` |
| Stacked area | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/stacked-area-chart.json` |
| Stacked bar | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/stacked-bar-chart.json` |
| Heatmap | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/heatmap.json` |
| Donut | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/donut-chart.json` |
| Sparkline | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/sparkline.json` |
| Brush | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/brush.json` |
| Bullet | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/bullet-chart.json` |
| Legend | `npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/legend.json` |

The registry's index, for `shadcn list` and shadcn's MCP server, is at `https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/registry.json`.

## How to Configure Time Scales
Britecharts has some logic to try guessing the best date format on time series charts from the time period of the dataset. As we haven't bulletproofed this algorithm, and sometimes users want specific formats, we also expose configuration options to set custom formats.

The next steps apply to time series charts like the line chart, stacked area chart and brush chart:
1. Render the chart using the default settings, see if the x-axis format is satisfactory. If not, keep on reading.
1. Check the chart's reference to find out the configuration options, for example, the [line chart reference][lineChartAPI]
1. Check the options within the `axisTimeCombinations` object of the chart instance:
```
console.log('combinations', line.axisTimeCombinations);
// Returns
{
    MINUTE_HOUR: 'minute-hour',
    HOUR_DAY: 'hour-daymonth',
    DAY_MONTH: 'day-month',
    MONTH_YEAR: 'month-year',
    CUSTOM: 'custom'
}
```
1. Set the `xAxisFormat` parameter to a value from the ones below (except 'custom')
1. Draw the chart and see if it meets your criteria. If not, try with other time combination. If still doesn't feel right, see next step.
1. Set the `xAxisFormat` parameter to the value `'custom'`
1. Set the `xAxisCustomFormat` parameter to a valid [D3.js time format specifier string][timeFormatSpecifiers]. For example: `line.xAxisCustomFormat('%H')`
1. Play around with different specifiers until finding something that works. You can experiment in [this block example][timeFormatsBlock].

Remember that for increased accuracy, all date formats in Britecharts should be provided in [ISO 8601 Extended Format][ISOFormat].


[gettingStarted]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/tutorials/getting-started
[colorPalettesDemo]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/storybook/core/?path=/story/attributes-colors--color-schemas
[colorsHelper]: https://github.com/britecharts/britecharts/blob/main/packages/core/src/charts/helpers/color.ts
[ISOFormat]: http://www.ecma-international.org/ecma-262/5.1/#sec-15.9.1.15
[lineChartAPI]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/line
[tooltipAPI]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/tooltip
[apiReference]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/bar
[formatSpecifiers]: https://github.com/d3/d3-format#locale_format
[formatLocale]: https://github.com/d3/d3-format#formatLocale
[storybook]: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/storybook/
